bib.title: Harnesses for Inference-Time Alignment over Execution Trajectories

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Harnesses for Inference-Time Alignment over Execution Trajectories", Boyuan Wang, Bochao Li, Minghan Wang (equal contribution), Yuxin Tao, Fang Kong. Southern University of Science and Technology. arXiv 2605.21516v1 [cs.LG], 15 May 2026. Preprint.

COVERAGE: all 35 of 35 pages (85,283 chars). Pages 25-33 are proofs, skimmed for results and found none. Pages 34-35 are prompt templates. Extraction was clean.

CORE CLAIM: A harness has two parts: a workflow (sub-goal decomposition) and guidance (reweighting of local actions). More structure is not monotonically better. Decomposition granularity must match the agent's controllable progress. Guidance helps only if it favours trajectories supported by evidence. "Partial harnessing" (scaffold only the first stages, then release the agent) can beat a full workflow. The theory is a stagewise recoverability model: P(success) is the product of per-stage recoverability probabilities.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (all small-scale, single-run)
- Terminal-Bench 2 granularity sweep: pass rate rises, then falls with sub-goal count k, "peaking at six steps" (p10).
  - Setup: planner qwen3.5-plus-02-15 writes a k-step workflow for k=1..10. Solver is GLM-5 (OpenRouter), run in Harbor Docker. 50 episodes per run, 1 attempt per (task,k) cell.
  - Tasks: 36 moderate-difficulty tasks, 32 in the aggregate curve. The 4 excluded tasks returned all zeros in the first trial.
  - Run locally on an M4 MacBook. No cost figure. No peak pass-rate value in the text (curve is in Fig 3a only).
- Plot-hallucination task (guidance): aligned guidance holds hallucination "near 0.35 regardless of count". Misaligned guidance rises "from 0.20 to nearly 0.90". Random interpolates (p10).
  - Setup: 6 chart types, k=0..10 guidance rules, 3 trials per k per chart type. LLM judge labels GROUNDED/HALLUCINATION/ERROR. The analysis and judge models are not named in the pages I read.
- Partial-harness case study: ONE task, llm-inference-batching-scheduler (official rate 80%). A 3-step partial harness (read inputs, list legal sizes, select shared shapes) completes. The full 10-step harness gets stuck in repeated revisions (p10-11). No pass rates, no n, no repeats.
- Synthetic addition task (G=100, tolerance 2): pass rate is non-monotonic in K, and the peak differs per agent. Pass rate is unimodal in the number of scaffolded chunks, and stronger agents peak earlier. Small, Medium and Large agents differ only in action scale (µ=6, 8, 10).

ABLATIONS (synthetic, App A.5)
- Retry budget R in 1..10: raises pass rate but saturates. "more attempts cannot fix a stage whose requested progress lies outside the agent's reachable scales" (p17).
- Completion tolerance: raises pass rate but accumulates terminal bias (p17-18).
- Guidance pruning: more pruning lowers pass rate, worst under fine decomposition.
- Chunk sizes c=10, 20, 25: the unimodal shape persists.
- Fig 9 repeats the granularity sweep with Qwen3.5-plus, GPT-OSS-120B and Gemini-3-flash as agents.
- There is no ablation of harness components on a real agent.

KEY QUOTES
- "more elaborate harnesses are not uniformly better: increasing decomposition or guidance can sometimes improve execution, but can also reduce final task success." (p1)
- "specifying only the initial steps and leaving the remaining execution to agent can achieve higher pass rate than fully structured workflows." (p1)
- "keep extending the harness only while the next scaffolded stage saves more residual risk than it introduces." (p7)
- "The right harness is the smallest one that keeps the agent on a recoverable trajectory, and no smaller." (p11)

LIMITS
- The authors concede "we adopt simplified settings and assumptions... real agent behavior is substantially more complex" (p11).
- The partial-harnessing claim on real data rests on one anecdotal task. There is no benchmark-level comparison of partial against full harnesses. The abstract overstates this.
- The Terminal-Bench result is n=1 attempt per cell with no confidence intervals. The authors do not report the number of valid cells per k.
- The sweep varies only the planner-written step count, with a fixed guidance block. It does not vary agent capability, so the "match to capability" link is shown only in synthetic data.
- Theorems 1-3 are informal and need strong assumptions: a recoverability tube, goal consistency, and diminishing returns on tail risk.
- "Guidance" in the synthetic runs is pruning of an action pool, which is far from real prompts.
- Nothing on multi-agent systems, subagents, role separation, topologies, handoffs or inter-agent failure modes. "Over-decomposition, over-pruning, hallucinated execution" are single-agent failure modes.
- Nothing on iterative simplification of a production harness.

PLACEMENT: Not 07-orchestration. It is single-agent workflow granularity, not multi-agent. It fits 08-maturity-and-failure-modes best (over-decomposition, over-pruning and hallucinated execution as failure modes, plus "when to stop adding scaffolding"). 02-harness-anatomy is a weaker second choice: the workflow/guidance split and the h=(κ,λ,ψ) parameters are a vocabulary for anatomy, but not a component inventory. At most a one-line "when not to over-decompose" cite in 07. Evidence quality is weak to moderate: theory is clean, real-data support is thin.

BUILDS ON
- Sutton, "The Bitter Lesson", 2019, as motivation.
- Plan-and-act (Erdogan et al., ICML 2025).
- DyFlow (Wang et al., 2025).
- ReAct (Yao et al., 2022).
- Harness-optimisation work: DSPy, GEPA, Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026), AgentSquare.
- Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026).
- The adjustable-autonomy and mixed-initiative literature: Horvitz 1999 and Scerri et al. 2002.
- Industry harness posts: Anthropic 2025 "Effective harnesses for long-running agents", OpenAI 2026 "Harness engineering", LangChain 2026 (Trivedy).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig 3a (p9), "On Terminal-Bench v2, pass rate first improves and then declines as the workflow is split into more steps." It is the only real-benchmark evidence and shows the inverted-U. Fig 4 (p10) is the more intuitive illustration of partial against full, but it is a single anecdote.
